summary: Describes the DDDS algorithm, which applies dynamically retrieved string transformation rules to an application-unique string. Well-formed rules reflect the delegation of management of the data tied to the string. It is part two of the DDDS series and replaces RFCs 2168 and 2915.

plainLanguage.summary: DDDS finds the answer to a string by following a trail of rules. It looks up a rule, applies that rule to the same starting string again, and repeats until a rule says the search is finished. The RFC defines only this general method, so it has to be read together with an application and a database from the rest of the series.

subtitle: How one string becomes an answer: look up a rule, apply it to that same string, and repeat until a rule says stop.

tldr.problem: Some identifiers, such as Uniform Resource Names, name a thing but carry no network location, so a client still has to find the server that holds data about them.
tldr.mechanism: DDDS keeps rewrite rules in a database. A first well known rule turns the application unique string into a key, the database returns the rules for that key, and each rule is applied to the original string until a terminal rule produces the final result.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3402 obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915. It defines only the general algorithm, so it is useful only together with an application and a database specified elsewhere in the DDDS series.

today: RFC 3402 is a Proposed Standard. The document states that it obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915 and updates RFC 2276. It is one part of the DDDS series, and the first part is RFC 3401.

sections.title: What DDDS Is For
sections.content:
The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) binds a string to data lazily, which means the binding is worked out at the moment it is needed instead of being stored in advance. A client starts with one unique string, looks up a rule for it, applies that rule to the same string, and repeats until a rule says it is the last one.

The idea came out of work on Uniform Resource Names (URNs). A URN says what something is but deliberately contains no network location, so a client that wants the data behind a URN has to find the server that holds it. The first system for this was the Resolver Discovery Service, which worked only with URNs. Other systems then applied the same algorithm to other kinds of identifier, so the specifications were rewritten to let new applications and rule databases be defined in a standard way.

This document covers only the general algorithm. It is part two of a series specified in RFC 3401, and the RFC warns that no document in the series can be understood without reading the others.
sections.plainLanguage: An identifier such as a URN can name something without giving any hint of where it lives. DDDS supplies a method for chasing that answer down, one rule at a time.

sections.title: The Words DDDS Uses
sections.content:
The RFC defines a small set of terms that the rest of the series reuses.

  • Application Unique String (AUS): the string the process starts with. Its lexical structure must imply a single delegation path.
  • Rewrite Rule: a rule applied to the AUS that gives either a new key for the next lookup or a final result for the calling application.
  • First Well Known Rule: a rule defined by the application rather than held in the database, used to produce the first valid key.
  • Terminal Rule: a rule whose output is the final result instead of another key.
  • Application: the protocols and specifications that fill in the general parts of the algorithm, including the AUS, the First Well Known Rule and the valid databases.
  • Rule Database: any store where a unique key identifies a set of rules.
  • Services and Flags: fields in a rule that let the application choose between branches and recognise terminal rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The vocabulary is small. The starting string is the application unique string, each lookup returns a rewrite rule, and the rule that ends the chain is the terminal rule.

sections.title: The Algorithm Step by Step
sections.content:
Rules live in a DDDS Rule Database and are fetched by key. One constraint matters most: a rule is never applied to the output of an earlier rule. Every rule is applied to the exact same AUS that the process started with.

  1. Apply the First Well Known Rule to the AUS to produce a key.
  2. Ask the database for the ordered set of rules bound to that key.
  3. Apply each rule's substitution expression, in order, to the AUS until one produces a non-empty string. If the list runs out with no match, tell the application that no valid output was available.
  4. If the rule's service description does not meet the client's needs, go back to step 3 and continue down the list. Otherwise use this rule.
  5. If the rule's flags say it is not terminal, go back to step 2 with the substitution result as the new key.
  6. Otherwise notify the application, giving it the flags and services of the rule and the output of the last substitution expression.

The algorithm assumes that everything needed for each delegation decision sits in the AUS and in the rule itself. It does not handle decisions that depend on knowledge from outside, such as the time of day, financial transactions or rights management.

Two notes come with the algorithm. First, when two rules count as equal, the priority field expresses a preference so that one rule can act as a fallback; the RFC says this is a preference, not a way of spreading load. Second, if a rule in the database expires while the process runs, the application must start again at step 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Every rule is applied to the string the process began with, never to the output of the rule before it. Each rule supplies the key of the next one, and the chain ends at a rule marked terminal.

sections.title: Rules and Substitution Expressions
sections.content:
A rule has four parts: a priority that shows which of two otherwise equal rules takes precedence, a set of flags that mark the rule's attributes and say whether it is terminal, a description of services that lets the application choose between delegation branches, and a substitution expression that does the actual string work.

The substitution expression combines a POSIX Extended Regular Expression with a replacement string, in the style of the Unix sed command. The first character of the expression is the delimiter, and the expression must contain exactly three unescaped occurrences of that delimiter. Digits must not be used as delimiters, because a backref would then be confused with a literal digit. The only flag defined is i, which asks for case-insensitive matching.

A backref from \1 to \9 in the replacement is filled with the text matched by the corresponding pair of parentheses in the expression. For the expression (A(B(C)DE)(F)G), \1 is ABCDEFG, \2 is BCDE, \3 is C and \4 is F. The result of applying a rule must be a key the database accepts, or, for a terminal rule, a valid output for the application, so clients should check the result before using it.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule is a pattern with a replacement attached. It matches part of the starting string and builds the next key from the pieces it found.

sections.title: Specifying an Application
sections.content:
The algorithm only becomes useful when an application and at least one database are written down. An application specification must define the Application Unique String, the First Well Known Rule, the valid databases and how the first key is made valid for each of them, and the expected output of a terminal rule. The URI Resolution application, for example, defines the AUS to be a URI and could define the first key as the characters before the first colon, which is the URI scheme.

No application may treat a key produced by a rule as the AUS for a new rule. The RFC says that leads to sendmail-style rewrite rules, which are fragile and error prone. There is one exception: a flag that suspends the rules and hands control to something outside DDDS, such as the p flag in URI Resolution, which marks the next step as protocol specific.

The priority field is only a way of saying that one rule is better, faster or cheaper than another. An application that needs to spread load between servers should do that outside DDDS. The RFC points at the DNS SRV record as one way of doing so.
sections.plainLanguage: The method on its own does nothing. A real use also needs a description of the starting string, the first rule, the databases that may be used, and the expected answer.

sections.title: Specifying a Database
sections.content:
Every application needs at least one database to fetch rules from, and one database can serve more than one application. A database specification must cover six things: a general specification, including the allowed character sets; the lookup procedure, which says how a query is formed and submitted; the key format; the rule format; the rule insertion procedure, which can include policy about which rules are allowed; and a method for avoiding rule collisions.

Collisions matter because several applications can share one database, ENUM and URI Resolution being the examples given. There are two usual ways to avoid them: a key is not allowed to be valid in two applications, or the regular expression matches enough of the AUS to tell the two applications apart. In the URI Resolution example the character set of a URI is 7-bit ASCII, which fits the 8-bit limit that DNS places on characters in its zone files.
sections.plainLanguage: A database description says how rules are stored and fetched, how they are written, and how two applications can share one store without giving the same key two meanings.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples, both invented for teaching and not based on any published application.

In the automobile parts example, the part number 4747301AB7D is the AUS. The first well known rule takes the first 5 digits, 47473, as the manufacturer ID and the key. The manufacturer's rule uses the next 3 digits to build a further query; in this example 01A names the Toyota line of cars. That rule delegates the query to a supply house in Japan and is marked terminal, so its result is the information about the part itself, held as EDIFAC data. The database is the APIDA Network, a network of EDI enabled databases that returns an XML encoded rewrite rule, and a manufacturer ID is only handed out to members of the Auto Parts Manufacturers Association.

In the document identification example, the AUS looks like <organization>-<department>-<author>:<project>-<bookcase>-<book>. The database is an LDAP directory, and the first key is the characters before the first hyphen. Delegation can run all the way down to the author's own document management environment, and the first section of the tree, the organization, is owned by the DIS Agency.
sections.plainLanguage: The first example treats a part number as an address made of several pieces. Each piece leads to the next, and the last piece is the answer itself.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short: the document only defines the algorithm, so by itself it implies no security issues. Real concerns can only be listed once the algorithm is joined to a particular database and application. The one risk the RFC names is that dynamic delegation points are a possible point of attack, because the rules are fetched on the fly.

The document creates no requirements on IANA. Database and application specifications may have considerable requirements, but they cannot be listed here.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules that are fetched on the fly can be tampered with. Where the rules live decides what checks are needed, so each application has to work that out for itself.

left.title: Non-terminal rule
left.desc: The output is a new key. The client looks that key up and applies the next rule to the same original string.

right.title: Terminal rule
right.desc: The output is the final result. The client hands it to the application along with the rule's flags and services.

items.title: Priority
items.text: Shows which of two otherwise equal rules takes precedence.

items.title: Flags
items.text: Mark attributes of the rule, including whether it is terminal.

items.title: Services
items.text: Describe the features of a delegation branch so the client can choose.

items.title: Substitution Expression
items.text: A POSIX Extended Regular Expression plus a sed-style replacement.

viz.caption: SUBSTITUTION EXPRESSION GRAMMAR, COPIED FROM THE RFC

data.title: subst-expr grammar
data.code:
subst-expr   = delim-char  ere  delim-char  repl  delim-char  *flags
delim-char   = "/" / "!" / <Any octet not in 'POS-DIGIT' or 'flags'>
ere          = <POSIX Extended Regular Expression>
repl         = *(string / backref)
string       = *(anychar / escapeddelim)
anychar      = <any character other than delim-char>
escapeddelim = "\" delim-char
backref      = "\" POS-DIGIT
flags        = "i"
POS-DIGIT    = "1" / "2" / "3" / "4" / "5" / "6" / "7" / "8" / "9"
